DAKOTA NEWS.
WASHINGTON, Feb. 11. The following resolutions were handed the president by the south eastern Dakota delegation yesterday:

Whereas, It is the earnest desire of the people of the Territory of Dakota residing south of the forty-sixth parallel that such part of said Territory should be formed into a State and admitted into the Union; and whereas, N. G Ordway, the present governor, has at sunday times and in divers ways, through self-sought press interviews, his annual report to the secretary of the interior and his letter to the president of the United States, possessed the people thereof as responsible and the legislature as mercury, and that an alarming financial and political condition exists therein; and whereas, by such representations the said Ordway has grossly defamed the people of the said Territory, and has greatly damaged the material interests of the same, has left his post of duty at the capitol of the Territory to give his entire time and attention to opposing admission whle pretending to favor 1; therefore be it

Resolved, That we, the delegates appointed by the convention of 500 members, represent all of the old counties comprising the proposed new State of Dakota, most urgently and respectfully recommend his immediate removal; and be it further

Resolved, That this delegation go as a body to the president of the United States and ask the removal of the governor of Dakota Territory as a measure of communities to the people of said Territory,

B. T. CAMPELL, Chairman.

EUGENE HUNTINGTON, Secretary.

Feb. 9, 1882.

The delegation, numbering about seventy members, called upon the president, and after formally presenting the matter for his consideration, retired with the understanding that he would meet a committee to-day. The committee, consisting of Maj. Kellam, chairman, Maj. Washburne, Messrs. Taylor, Cook and Sterling, called on the president to-day and had a full and satisfactory hearing.

THANKING PETTIGREW.

At a meeting of the delegates from North Dakota the following resolution was unanimously adopted:

Resolved, That the thanks of Northern Dakota are due and hereby tendered the Hon. R. F Pettigrew for his valuable aid in presenting the claims of that section of Dakota to a separate Territorial government, and for the uniform kindness and courtesy shown by him to the delegation.

Resolved, further, That this preamble and resolution be signed by the chairman and secretary of the delegation and that a copy thereof be presented to Mr. Pettigrew.

A. H. BARNES, Chairman,

F. H. ADAMS, Secretary.

THE ENABLING ACT.

WASHINGTON, Feb. 11. The sub-committee of the house committee on Territories have agreed to report to the full committee on Tuesday next in favor of the proposition to admit as a State all that portion of Dakota lying south of the forty-sixth parallel of latitude: the northern portion to constitute a new Territory of Dakota. Joseph Budd, in jail at Yankton for the murder of C. A. Borst, four years ago has been released on his own recognizance, pending the arrival of two important witnesses.

A negro barber broke into the residence of Mrs. Merrill of Watertown and attempted to rape her, but her cries brought asistance and the negro fled. A posse of citizens are after him and if caught will be dealt with in a summary inner.

It is intimated that Strang of Pennsylvania will succeed John B. Raymond as marshal of Dakota.

The noted character and so-called heroine of the Black Hills and frontier, Calamity Jane, has arrived in Bismarck.

A very large citizens' meeting was held at Deadwood to discuss the question of bonding the counties of the Hills to aid the railroad company first constructing a railroad to the Hills. Much enthusiasm prevailed. The sentiment was in favor of building from the Northern Pacific at Cheveune, which latter city voted $400,000 for the same purpose. A committee of fifteen was appointed to procure a line of action.

A delegation from southeastern Dakota waited upon the president last Friday, and asked for the removal of Gov. Ordway.

At Sioux Falls, a dwelling upon Phillips avenue, owned by Mrs. Schuntzeler and occupied by Edward Burns, was burned. Loss, $600; insured for $150.

Yankton Press: The Milwaukee road is making preparations to extend south beyond Ashton in the early spring, to connect at Huron with its Jim River branch from Yankton north. The Northwestern is also building westward from Watertown through Clark county, and will probably connect with its Ordway branch at Redfield, though, of course, nothing is definitely known relative to the movements of the road west of Clark Center, aside from the survey to Redfield.

Emigration to the James River Valley via the Hastings & Dakota division of the Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul, has already commenced, the new settlers are daily arriving from Michigan, Wisconsin and Iowa. The great majority appear to be intelligent and in very comfortable circumstances—just the kind to make the Jim River prairies blossom beautifully.

A Washington special says that the proposition to establish a new land district in Dakota, with office at Jamestown, has every prospect of success.

Alexander H. Stevens says he will support measures for the division and admission of Dakota. He takes a broad and statismanlike view of the question.

In sinking a well on the tarm of Mr. Moore, twelve miles from Wahpeton, at the depth of 175 feet was struck a vein of water which thruws a full round stream twenty feet in the air, forming, as it wore, the finest artesian well in the great northwest.

A crazy fireman on the Northern Pacific freight train, near Alsop, recently, overpowered the engineer and undertook to run the train to suit his own idea of speed—about a mile a minute. The engineer finally succeeded in stopping the train just in time to save a collision, but had his coat and vest torn off by the maniac. As soon as the train was stopped the lunatic started across the prairie and has not since been seen.

Wm. A Moore has sold his paper, the Ordway (Dak.) Times, to Messrs. Elliott & Howard.

Ole Oleson Tol of Flandrau was kicked by a horse on Wednesday and died the following day.

Lawrence county has a debt of $550,000, which costs 10 per cent. interest.

Dell Rapids hopes to have 1,000 inhabitants before the end of the year.

The body of Wild Bill, who was killed by Jack McCall at Deadwood, Black Hills, in 1876, was buried in the old cemetery at that place and two years afterward removed to the new burial grounds further out of town. Upon removing the coffin lid his remains were found solitified, with fea-ca

tures as perfect as the day upon which the funer. occurred.

A reporter of the Fargo Argus interviewed Hon. J. W. Fisher, who came in from Casselton, regarding the Callins-Slingsby case, which has been creating some excitement there. Mr. Fisher states that the preliminary examination closed in the presence of a large audience, and that Justice Lawrence's decision that these was no cause of action met with such universal approval that Slingsby was carried from the hails of justice to his residence on the shoulders of the people. The impression prevails that some one desirous of securing the position of postmaster, which Mr. Slingsby has filled for some time past, originated the scandal, hoping for a change. The verdict of Justice Lawrence seems to meet the general approval of the people of Casselton.

hail-brothers-centreville-1882-02.A1:
Negroes Waylaid and Shot.
St. Louis, Feb. 19.—A terrible tragedy occurred yesterday near Centerville, Tex., in which two negroes named Hall were killed and their wives mortally wounded. It appears the negroes, who were riding along the road in a wagon, had some trouble with the child of a white man named Lyle. The child ran home and told its father about the affair and the latter, taking a shot gun, concealed himself by the roadside. Shortly after the negroes came by and Lyle fired upon them from his ambush almost blowing the heads off the men and fatally wounding the women. The murderer fled but officers started in pursuit.

Chelsea, a Boston suburb, was visited by a $25,000 fire on the 17th.

Two deaths from smallpox and ten new cases of the disease were reported in Chicago last Friday. Of the latter, two were of tramps, who came from the country.

JUAN GARCIA, a noted horse thief, was killed at San Antonio, Texas, on the 16th, while resisting arrest.

At Louisville the river is up to the second story windows of some of the houses on the levee, and business in that portion of the city is entirely suspended.

O. B. Potter, who owned the World Building in New York, which burned a few days ago, owing to a defective flue, will have to answer before the Grand Jury for his neglect in not repairing it. He is on bail for $5,000.

Geo. Cunningham's house, at Ameliasburg, Ohio, burned Sunday. Three children perished.

The Albion print works, at Philadelphia, burned Monday, and the charred body of an unknown man was found on one of the floors. Several others are missing.

The latest estimate of the loss at Haverhill places it at $2,225,000, with an insurance of $2,000,000.

The Nebraska star-routers will next be tried on the charge of having made false returns to the Government.

At Painesville, Ohio, Martin Noonan has been convicted of robbing the American Express company of $21,000 in 1878.

A fine line of "Mother Hubbard" Collars, cheaper than elsewhere, at the Odd Cent Store.

The doorkeeper of the skating rink at Providence has been held for trial for refusing entrance to a negro who had bought a ticket.

Two men have been sentenced to the New York State prison for violation of the election laws. The offense was committed in 1879.

Grain contracts for February were declared suspended on the Cincinnati call board, on account of the submerged condition of railroads.

On the Alton track, at a point one mile south of Joliet, on Sunday, some rails were found tied down in such a manner as to have ditched the night express.

In a hotel at Louisville a desperate fight took place between John Wyatt, famous as a deputy marshall, and two city officers. Fourteen shots were fired, Wyatt being mortally wounded.

A watchman on the steamship Niagara, at New York, saw a stranger come on board with twenty pounds of gunpowder, and an investigation revealed the presence of sixty pounds in the mess-room.

Indiana has now a school population of 714,343, and expended in public instruction during the past year $1,307,-210.20. Her total receipts for school purposes were $5,845,420.54. The school enrollment last year was 503,855.

Henry Hill, who was put off of a Georgia railroad train last summer because he insisted on riding with his coat off, though the conductor instructed him that it was impolite to the women in the car, has obtained a verdict for $5,000 against the company.

The Louisville, New Albany and Chicago road reports gross earnings for 1881 of $947,654. When completed for 450 miles the indebtedness will be $53,000,000 in bonds and $5,080,000 stock. Four thousand tons of steel rails were purchased and laid during the year.

The outlook for winter wheat in a number of counties in the southern part of Kansas is pronounced better than ever before at this season of the year. Farmers are already plowing for corn, gardening operations have begun, and nothing but exceptionally cold weather in March can prevent early seeding and a bountiful crop.

The Presbyterian clergymen of Chicago, at their weekly meeting Monday, adopted the report of a committee that the theater as managed there is an open gateway of perdition, and its influences are inimical to Christian homes. It was also voted that reporters should not be admitted to the meetings, only one protest being made.

A feud growing out of a trivial circumstance developed into a fearful tragedy at Centreville, Tex., last Saturday. Two negroes had some words with the child of a white man named Lyle, who seized his shotgun and lay in ambush along the roadside, and when the colored men with their wives rode past in a wagon, he fired on them, killing both men and mortally wounding the two women.

The rainfall at St. Louis in thirty-six hours was over six inches. There were ten landslides on the Missouri Pacific road, and an Iron Mountain freight train is caught at Cliff cave. Alton, Indianapolis, and Burlington tracks are submerged near Mitchell. The ferry docks at St. Charles were swept away,

President Arthur gave his first State dinner on the 17th.
Edmunds' anti-polygamy bill passed the Senate unanimously.
At Washington on Sunday the churches adopted anti-polygamy resolutions.
Thirteen moonshiners and a quantity of whisky have been captured in Texas.
Two editors, in Mexico, recently fought a duel with pistols. Both fired and both fell dead.
The Mississippi levees are giving away to the floods, and towns and farms are being inundated.
Track laying commenced Monday on the Southern Pacific branch from Mohave to the Colorado river.
An explosion in the pyrotechnic works at Chester, Pa., on the 17th, killed 15 persons and wounded 70 or 80 others.
A Portland dispatch says that the Board of Trade passed resolutions urging the abrogation of the Hawaiian reciprocity treaty.

The circulation of standard silver dollars for the week ending February 18th, was $135,485, against $92,49, for the corresponding period of 1881.

Gen's Sherman and Pope and Col. Marrow start the 1st. of March on a tour of inspection to the department of Texas, New Mexico and Arizona.

London Times Berlin correspondence: Bismarck has conferred with the Emperor regarding Skobeloft's sdeech. A mild remonstrance will probably be sent to St. Petersburg.

There is great excitement in the neighborhood of Desmoines, Iowa, on the discovery of a vein of pure Cannel coal 5 feet thick, also a six foot vein of Bituminous.

The Director of the Mint has just decided that coin once punched or mutilated can only be considered as bullion hereafter even if the holes are filled with the same quality of metal.
Last Saturday the Massachusetts State Senate passed a resolution expressing abhorrence of the practice of polygamy. Congressman are aaked to secure the passage of anti-polygamy law.

A St. Petersburg dispatch says: The reported outrage upon the Jews near Kicheneff is confirmed. The affair grew out of an elopement and marriage of a Jewish maiden with a Christian.

A Helena, Ark., dispatch says: Disasters from the flood are still increasing. Cattle and hogs have been drowned by the hundreds, and many buildings swept away. In some localities the people are threatened by starvation.

A tramp printer from Kentucky by the name of R. D. Raven got into a quarrel with James Cook at Waverly, Nebraska, and drew a revolver and shot him dead. Raven was taken to Lincoln to save him from being lynched.

The water in all Northwestern Texas streams is rising rapidly and flooding the country. Two big bridges on the Texas Pacific Railroad have been swept away between Weatherford and Fort Worth, stopping travel.

A fire in Haverhill, Mass., last Saturday destroyed the best portion of the town. Some 80 shoe firms were burned out and others injured more or less. Two or three lives lost and 2,000 persons thrown out of employment. Loss estimated at $2,500,-000.

A Portland dispatch says: The British ship Corsia struck on the Columbia river bar last night while coming out. She was abandoned during the night and sank this morning. The crew were saved. She had a cargo of wheat for the United Kingdom, valued at $53,000.

A Cincinnati dispatch says: It has been raining hard all day with a prospect of continuing. The River is rising at the rate of an inch per hour. It is already the highest since 1847. Indications give the opinion that it will exceed the rise of 1830 the greatest on record. Navigation is closed.

Gov. Cameron and party last Saturday captured a whole oyster fleet, consisting of six schooners and one sloop, and made prisoners of the crews—sixty-one men
The British Connsel reports there is a movement to exaggerate the seriousness of the anti-Jewish riots in Russia. The loss of life and outrages on women are generally denied. The destruction of Jewish property is fully confirmed. The statement is confirmed about 100 Jews being shamefully maltreated at Warsaw, and ten or twelve who died of their injuries.

The House, on the 20th, on motion of Page, suspended the rules and adopted a resolution making making the Chinese immigration bill a special order for the second Tuesday in March and from day to day thereafter until finally disposed of, but not to interfere with the consideration of the several appropriation bills. The vote on adopting the resolution was 118 against 31.

Deposits of gold nuggets were received at the New York assay office office this week, varying from mere grains to the size of new eggs. The largest one weighed 23 ounces and was worth over $430. The total weight after melting was 848 troy ounces, and the gold bullion was worth $15,934. These nuggets came from California, and were obtained from "pockets" by hydraulic process.

lewis-smith-arkadelphia-1882-03-09.A1:
ARKADELPHIA, ARK.
Three Negroes Shot by Two White Men.
St. Louis, March 7.—A special from Arkadelphia, Ark., says: A shooting affray occurred six miles south of here in which three negroes, named Lewis Smith, Aaron Dark and Ed Clark, were shot by two white men—Joe Ross and Bud Henry. The first named negro was killed outright, the second shot six times and cannot possibly recover, while the third was shot twice and may recover. The shooting arose out of a quarrel while working on the settlement roads. The white men escaped.

The first-named negro was killed outright; the second was shot six times, and cannot possibly recover, while the third, shot twice, may recover. lewis-smith-arkadelphia-1882-03-09.A6:
Tragical Tales.
At a dance at the house of John Mooney, in Indian Territory, on the night of the 10th inst., two young men named Montgomery and Horton got into a quarrel, which ended in both drawing pistols and shooting several times at each other. Montgomery was killed outright and Horton mortally wounded.

Two laborers named Monahan and MacAvoy quarreled at Steubenville, O., on the 11th inst. The latter was fatally stabbed.

At Linkville, Oregon, on the night of the 11th inst., a mob of masked men attempted to take a murderer named H. C. Lewis from the jail. Lewis fired on the mob, who responded with a volley, which killed the deputy sheriff and wounded Justice Wright. The would-be lynchers then retired.

A terrible tragedy was enacted at a school house at Harrisburg, Pernsett County, Ark., on the 7th inst. County Treasurer J. J. Smith remonstrated with the teacher for whipping his child. The conversation became heated and finally led to Smith's striking E. J. Wilmot, the teacher, on the head with a billet of wood, crushing his skull. The injured man died in three hours.

In a drunken quarrel at New Orleans on the night of the 7th inst., Richard Shea was stabbed to death by James Cosgrove.

An aged couple named O'Massey, living near Charlottesville, Va., were found murdered on the morning of the 8th inst., in their house. Money was the object.

A mob took Charles Shelton, John Redmond and Harry French from the jail at Los Lunas, Cal., on the 8th inst., and hung them to a tree.

A courtesan named Mary Sigman and her mother were assassinated at Mount Vernon, Ky., on the 8th inst.

A remarkable story comes from the City of Mexico. The report is that highwaymen attacked a stage full of armed men and that eleven of the outlaws were killed.

It is reported that nine Europeans journeying from Tunis to Gafsa were murdered between Tunis and Kairwan.

Advices from New Mexico are to the effect that Deputy Sheriff Miers and Martinez with a posse were attacked by Pueblo Indians while attempting to arrest some of the Pueblos who had escaped from jail. Miers was killed and Martinez mortally wounded.

A shocking tragedy took place at Boston, Mass., on the 7th inst. Mrs. Harriet Bell while returning from a grocery store near her home was accosted by an unknown man who followed her to the doorstep of her home and then cut her throat. She lived but a short time. The assassin escaped.

A brace of cattle thieves named Arnold Howard and Frank Young, in jail at Del Noter, Col., were visited by a mob on the 7th inst. Howard was killed outright and Young mortally wounded.

An affray with pistols took place at Arkansas City, on the 5th inst., in which J. W. Hale was killed by John Fuller.

Three negroes—Lewis Smith and Aaron and Ed. Clark—were killed in an affray at Arkadelphia, Ark., on the 6th inst. The shooting was done by Joe Ross and Thad. Henry, both white.

Tax Collector Robert Taylor was shot dead by Dr. Sims at Perryville, Perry County, Ark., on the 4th inst.

Bud Harris a young white man who mysteriously disappeared in Rome about two weeks ago, was found dead in the river.

General Toombs does not agree with Attorney General Anderson in his opinion as to the invalidity of the lessees of the State road.

Munroe Bloom, colored, was shot and killed at Morrow's Station on the Central railroad, Thursday by Constable Felix Anderson. He was resisting arrest.

A man by the name of Jones living near Sheffield, in Cain Creek district, ploughed up a glass jar in his field a few days ago containing several thousand dollars in gold.

The jury in the trial of Egbert Stevenson, charged with murdering his aunt in Gwinnett county last summer, returned a verdict of guilty, and the prisoner was sentenced to be hanged. He confessed.

The Constitution says: "Gen. P. M. B. Young will certainly be a candidate for Congress at large, and Judge J. W. H. Underwood will probably contest the mountain delegations with him."

An incorrigible little darkey, a thief from boyhood, of Walker county, named Andy Hall, only ten years old, was sentenced to the penitentiary of Dade coal pits for five years, at the recent session of the Superior Court in that county, for stealing a horse.

T. A. Bean, who deserted his wife at Newnan a few days ago and went to Atlanta with a depraved female, was tried at Newnan last Tuesday for wife desertion, found guilty and sentenced to the chain gang for 12 months.

A novel suit has been started by a citizen of Atlanta. He has been unable, after two years of trial, to get place for his children in the public schools. He now proposes to resist the payment of the school tax by law, and has employed an attorney to take the matter in hand.

Dublin Gazette: We learn that the candidates for the Legislature from this county, are as thick as the hairs on a dog's back. In fact, we learn that every man who can spell baker and give out an old fashioned hymn, is a candidate before the dear people.

James White, of Dalton, while preparing his gun for hunting last Friday, rested it upon a vat's edge, at White's tannery, to remove a wadding, and upon suddenly turning it fell into the vat, striking the hammer and discharging the gun in its decent. A load passed through White's left arm, grazing his side. The wounded member is much swollen and inflamed, and amputation will perhaps be necessary.

Commissioner Henderson said to a Constitution reporter: "The decrease in the sale of fertilizers this year is surprising. There has been less sold so far than for the same period at any time in the last eight years. The price varies in different localities, and in some places standard fertilizers sell as low as four hundred pounds of middling cotton per ton."

Cartersville Free Press: Work on the ore banks at Bartow iron works has been suspended on account of a mortgage of $60,000 being foreclosed. Your Uncle Joseph E. Brown swooped down upon it. We have not as yet learned when operations will again commence. The car factory is working on full time, although without as many hands as before the explosion, the engine not being of sufficient power to work so many. Their new engine will probably arrive within a month.

We learn that the man, Peter Corbin, charged with committing an outrage on a lady in Gilmer county, who was arrested in this place week before last by deputy marshal King and turned over to the sheriff of said county, mention of which was made in this paper, was taken from the Gilmer county jail, the night after the sheriff returned to Ellijay with him, by a party of masked men and was found the next day in a piece of woods near the town with his head completely severed from his body. We are opposed to lynch law under any circumstances, and hope the story is not true.—Dalton Citizen.

The dwelling of Mrs. Thomas Macey, near Sulphur Spring, Meriwether county, was destroyed by fire on Wednesday.

A negro named D. Nance was seriously hurt while hauling timber for Mr. J. I. Kemp, near McVille, on Monday last.

The Rome Bulletin learns that twenty-six new engines have been ordered for the Rome extension of the Macon and Brunswick Road. Rogers & Cook's make were ordered, owing to the fact that the Baldwin Works are overrun with orders.

A little son of Mr. A. J. Buchanan, of Americus, was tossed by a vicious cow, one day last week. He was not much hurt, however.

Mr. A. J. Ronder, an old citizen of Heard county, was found recently lying in a gully and greatly exhausted. He had been very feeble for some time, and it is supposed fell down and could not help himself. The exposure was so great that he died shortly after being conveyed home.

Mr. Michael Hartley died recently, in Crawford county, at the age of ninety-seven years.

Mr. David Robinson writes from Albany, under date of Saturday, as follows: "A fine stream of water now flows from our artesian well at a depth of 580 feet. The water commenced to flow to-day at noon. We are still drilling deeper for a stream of more force."

Wiregrass Watchman: "The Darien timber market is very low and we can't for the life of us see why people will persist in cutting it. Timber at the present prices and guano together is fast running this section of Georgia."

Sylvania Telephone: "A very touching scene was witnessed at the Methodist Church in this place on Sunday night last, when the pastor requested the congregation to kneel in prayer for our stricken Representative. There was not one of the large congregation but what knelt without hesitation, and a more sincere and general feeling of sympathy we have never seen."

Americus Recorder: "While the Wide Awakes were throwing water last Thursday the pipemen swung their nozzle around in a half circle, and as the sun shone upon the falling spray a beautiful rainbow appeared, extending the distance of about 200 feet, and making an arch about forty feet high. Athens Banner-Watchman: "There are not a more orderly and well-behaved set of young men in the South than the students at the State University. They are quiet, sober and gentlemanly and attract the attention of strangers by their deportment. We do not know a young man in the University who is addicted to drink or dissipation. They are certainty a credit to the State and to themselves."

Hampton Weekly: "Last Friday night some party or parties forced an entrance into the Arcade saloon and feloniously purloined several packages of choice liquor, six dollars in money and a fine breech-loading shotgun belonging to Mr. E. R. James. Entrance was effected by means of a large rock, with which the door was beaten in, and which was found lying on the three-hold next morning. This occurred in the full glare of a street lamp, which stood not more than twenty feet away."

Cedartown Advertiser: "On Thursday evening last, as the young sons of Dr. Chas. H. Harris were riding his horses to water at Cedar creek and were going at a very rapid pace, Seals, who is about eleven years old, saw the horse he was riding about to go between two trees, and endeavored to rein him so as to avoid them. He was unable to do so, and came in such violent contact with one of the trees that his leg was broken above the knee. He has had the best of attention, and at last accounts was doing well."

Augusta News: "A gentleman from Burke county informs the News this morning that forest fires for several days past have been very destructive to fences, woods, corded wood, and in one instance a residence was destroyed, being that known as the Goff house, some miles from Waynesboro. In the neigh borhood of Green's Cut Dr. Powell and Captain Walton lost large y in fencing, as also did Mr. Pink Thomas and others. Great quantities of corded wood have been destroyed. Mr Keener, living near this city, has lost thirty cords recently."

Cochran Enterprise: "One negro shot and killed another on Tuesday last at Bishop & Co.'s mill, near No. 12 (Chauncey), M. & B. R. R. The two quarreled and one of them started for his gun, which was a short distance away, and the other drew his little pistol and shot at him twice, one ball striking him in the back and coming out just above the navel. He got his gun, but when he got back his antagonist had fled the field. When our informant left, a few hours after, the wounded man was dying. The murderer is still at large. We could not learn the names of the parties."

Meriwether Vindicator: "Charlie, son of Mr. W. P. Findley, has been spending several months at Senoia with his grandfather, Mr. J. B. Heard. Recently the boy ran down to the train to mail a letter. The letter being mailed, the little boy stepped back to the platform, and overcome by his exertion in running, as it is supposed, he swooped and fell to the ground, a distance of several feet. In falling his breast struck the end of a crosstie. Since that time Charlie has lost all appetite, and is frequently attacked with such paroxysms of pain as to render his screams almost heart-rending. He is carefully attended by Dr Brantley, who pronounced his case a most singular one."

Columbus Times: "Mr. Fred, Little, of Allen's Station, Richmond county, said in his essay at the Georgia Agricultural Convention, in Augusta: 'In his opinion the best land for watermelon culture was a sandy loam, and if possible, a place which had laid out for some time, and had grown up in small pines and broom sedge. He then proceeded to give his method of culture. When the plants are well established they should be thinned down to one plant to a hill if large melons are desired, and this is very requisite if the melons are intended for sale.' The most popular melon in this market the past season was the Mountain Sweet and a long white or gray rhind, and we hope the market gardeners will be prepared to supply the market with fine ones the present season, hence we publish the above."

Rome Bulletin, 24th: "Yesterday afternoon quite a serious accident happened to Mr. J. Monroe Neal, of Cartersville. He had engaged a horse from one of our livery stables for the purpose of going out into the country to see Mr. Mitchell. Just as he got opposite Messrs. King & Bros' store, the horse was moving at a pretty lively speed, when Mr. Neal, not wanting to go so fast, gave the rein a sudden jerk, the horse rearing up and falling backwards, throwing Mr. Neal to the ground. He was assisted into Langey's store and Dr. Hoyt was summoned immediately. After a careful examination it was found that he had sustained a severe sprain in the small of the back. Besides this he suffered from acute pains in his feet, the horse having fallen across them. As good luck would have it, he fell a little to one side, thereby saving his life, as the horse fell directly backward. Mr. Neal is a prominent young attorney from Cartersville."

In the immediate vicinity of Natchez there have been hundreds, and we may probably be speaking within bounds when we say thousands, of these beautiful animals, which have crossed the river within the space of a few miles above and below this city. Worn and exhausted as they have been, after their long swim across the swollen river, they would have fallen an easy prey to the pot-hunters who only hunt for profit, had it not been for the extraordinary exertions of the true sportsmen of the county, and humane people who despise wanton cruelty. On Sunday last, several gentlemen found a number of deer that had fallen into a ravine, from which they found it impossible to get out. With true humanity they went to work and dug a pathway by which the little animals could find their way out of the ravine, helped them to mount to the top of the bank, and sent them on their way rejoicing to the green woods of the country. Instances of the same kind of humane feeling have been, we are glad to say, the rule with the people of this vicinity, while the disposition to capture and kill the deer has been the exception. —Natchez Democrat.

At Burkeville, Newton County, Tex., there is on the premises of Judge M. D. Hines a well of ordinary width and depth, to obtain water from which two buckets are used. These are connected by a rope, which passes over a wheel suspended from a frame above the curbing. The contrivance is a simple one, the arrangements being such that as one bucket is drawn up the other descends. The strange feature about the well is that at irregular periods, and without any visible or known cause, the buckets will change places, the empty one descending to the bottom and the filled one rising to the top of the well.

Mrs. Coker, with her three children, in an ox-cart, was recently returning home from Perry, Ga. The road they traveled passed through very rank wire-grass, which had been set on fire. In trying to get out of the way the cart and oxen became fastened among pine logs, and the fire overtook them. The cart, with the two children inside, was consumed and the oxen were burned to death. The woman attempted to escape with her infant, but her clothing caught fire and she and the other child were so badly burned that they have since died.

A novel suit has been entered by a citizen of Atlanta, Ga. He has been unable, after two years of trial, to get a place in the public schools. He now proposes to resist the payment of the school-tax by law, and has employed an attorney to take the matter in hand. He says: "I do not see why I should be taxed to support the schools when I can not get any representation in them. I have the same right of any other citizen to send my boy, and yet there are hundreds of others who get schooling and I have none. I do not think they can collect a school-tax when they refuse to let me send my son to the school."

The owner of the cave deposits of bat guano in Uvalde County, Texas, says the supply can not be exhausted in a century. An analysis shows over 11 per cent. of ammonia. The caves have recently been reached by railroad tracks, and the first shipment has been made. The product is expected to bring $50 per ton.

For several months says the Conyers (Ga.) Weekly, one of our citizens has been noticing that his butcher invariably let his hand rest on the meat slightly when he weighed it, and he reweighed it at home and found it from a half to a pound short. He kept an account of these deficiencies, and when they aggregated one hundred pounds he took out an attachment for the butcher's hand, claiming that it rightly belonged to him, he having more than paid for it.

The region south of Memphis is swarming with buffalo-gnats, which are killing what little stock was saved from drowning.

The New Orleans Gas-Light Company has been declared by Judge Pardee to have no legal existence.

Out of a total vote of 640, Bryan, Tex., gave a majority of 377 for liquor prohibition.

A convicted horse-thief named Bondy jumped from a train near San Antonio, Tex., last week, and was shot dead by the guards.

Two negroes, who were resisting arrest for forgery, were shot by a constable at Morrow's Station, Ga., a few days ago. Both escaped, but one, named Bloom, was afterward found dead in the woods. The negroes had first shot at the constable.

One hundred families have moved into Birmingham, Ala., since the 1st of December.

Gov. Colquitt, of Georgia, has determined not to call an extra session of the Legislature for the purpose of redistricting the State.

Eighty-five thousand tons of fertilizers were sold in North Carolina for the year 1881.

Silk culture in Louisiana has of late become a thriving industry, and promises an abundant production.

In 1865 Florence, S. C., contained only ten houses. It now has a population of over 2,000, and last year over 100 houses were built.

A Justice of the Peace in Atascosa County, Texas, says that he has assessed but two fines for misdemeanors during eight years.

Watermelons are up and doing well in Georgia. Three hundred acres are planted in Brooks County.

Representative Black, of Georgia, is seriously ill. He is not expected to recover.

Macon, Ga., had a $50,000 fire the other day, and Mr. R. B. Watson, cotton broker, perished in the flames.
Floriada is full of tourists.
During the past week, says the Greenville (N. C.) News, about 140 colored people have left this section for points west and south. It has been developed upon investigation that labor bureaus are in active operation in Texas and Louisiana, which have been organized for the purpose of meeting the large demand made by sugar and cotton planters in those States for laborers.
Isidore Levy, of New Orleans, who was arrested for arson at the instance of the insurance companies and was acquitted, has brought suit against the underwriters for $100,000.
Faber gets the wood for his pencils from Cedar Keys, Fla.
A company proposes to supply the city of Atlanta, Ga., with water by a canal and aqueduct of forty miles from the River Chattahoochee. The cost of the undertaking will be $2,500,000, and the revenue will come from the use of the water by the city and the rent of power to private enterprises.
